purpose: Reconstruct which essential household burdens showed the earliest measurable post-shock pressure after the March 2026 shipping/diesel shock without treating CPI as the governing household-welfare metric and without equating lower purchased quantity with lower underlying need.
governing_distinctions: higher mandatory essential costs can compress purchasing power in another essential category without reducing underlying need
ordering of observable burden is distinct from causal attribution

shock_clock.basis: USDA-documented marine bunker-fuel shock already preserved in the calibration lane
shock_clock.rule: Both clocks remain visible; no result may be promoted by selecting the more favorable clock after observing outcomes.

observed_lanes.causal_note: Observed rapid consumer motor-fuel price pressure contemporaneous with the broader energy shock; this alone does not isolate shipping or diesel as sole cause.

National electricity and utility-gas indexes show continuing essential-cost burden but do not establish the first downstream manifestation of the March shipping/diesel shock. Local delivery/transmission fees can diverge materially from national averages and are not captured here at household-contract granularity.
March monthly CPI did not show food first, while the year-over-year price level remained elevated; April showed renewed monthly grocery-price increase.

observations.confounder: Easter/calendar shift materially affects year-over-year comparison

observed_lanes.causal_note: Spending growth with flat/falling units is consistent with constrained real food acquisition. It does not establish reduced underlying food demand and does not by itself isolate diesel/shipping as the cause.

cross_lane_ordering_assessment.food_consumer_price_signal: not_first_under_monthly_national_CPI; renewed increase visible in April
cross_lane_ordering_assessment.food_real_acquisition_signal: already constrained/flat before and during March, so it cannot be cleanly dated as a new post-shock effect from aggregate year-over-year scanner data alone
cross_lane_ordering_assessment.utilities: national essential-cost pressure present, but current evidence does not establish them as the first downstream March-shock manifestation
cross_lane_ordering_assessment.reason: The available lanes use different measurement systems, temporal grains, and baselines. A single ordinal winner would overstate comparability.

bounded_finding: The March-April evidence supports a coherent sequence in which a large diesel/energy shock and transportation/distribution cost increases were visible before a clean national monthly food-price acceleration. At the household level, food affordability was already strained: national grocery prices remained above year-earlier levels while food-and-beverage units were flat or falling relative to dollars spent. The evidence therefore strengthens the broader essential-cost and food-system transmission mechanism but does not establish that food consumer prices were the first downstream burden observed, nor that lower food-unit purchases reflect lower underlying food demand.
nonimplications: Do not infer that household need for food, electricity, fuel, or water declined because observed quantity consumed or purchased declined.
Do not infer that CPI is a household purchasing-power measure.
Do not infer that national utility indexes capture local regulated delivery/transmission fees or individual contracted bill structures.
Do not infer sole or dominant diesel causation from temporal alignment alone.
Do not promote this record to a person-level credibility score.
